explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. Mordecai, the Jew who wrote the letters, sets up an "annual celebration" on the fourteenth and fifteenth days of Adar (Esther 9:21). Annual means it comes around again and again. He didn't plan a party for one afternoon. He put it on the calendar in ink.

A parade is one afternoon of confetti and sore feet, and then everybody goes home. Mordecai's letters ask for something bigger. He sets up an "annual celebration" on the fourteenth and fifteenth days of Adar (Esther 9:21). It's a yearly party, not a single parade.

explanations.answer: A new tax for the palace
explanations.explanation: Nobody opens a letter hoping for a tax bill, so I get the guess. But these letters are about a celebration. Mordecai, the Jew who wrote them, sets up an "annual celebration" on the fourteenth and fifteenth days of Adar (Esther 9:21). He's asking people to throw a party, not pay for one.

Joy is right, baker. Mordecai writes that this is "…the month in which their sorrow turned to joy and their mourning into a holiday." Think about that swap. Sorrow walked in the door and joy walked out wearing its coat. These days were set up to remember that turn.

Fear is a fair guess, baker, but the letter names something else. Mordecai writes that this is the month "…in which their sorrow turned to joy and their mourning into a holiday." (Esther 9:22). Joy is the word the text gives.

Anger is a reasonable guess, friend. But look at the words Mordecai chose. He writes that their "…sorrow turned to joy and their mourning into a holiday." (Esther 9:22). He wrote that these were to be days of feasting and joy.

True, friend. Mordecai wrote "…that these were to be days of feasting and joy, of sending gifts to one another and to the poor." So the party doesn't stay at your own table. It reaches your neighbors and the poor too. That's a celebration with the front door wide open.

This one is true, so you can relax. Mordecai wrote "…that these were to be days of feasting and joy, of sending gifts to one another and to the poor." Gifts are part of the plan, and so is thinking of the poor. I'd call that a very well-planned holiday.

Not quite, baker, and the text says the opposite. "So the Jews agreed to continue the custom they had started, as Mordecai had written to them." (Esther 9:23). They had already started the custom, and they agreed to continue it. Agreeing is the opposite of refusing.

False is right. The text says, "So the Jews agreed to continue the custom they had started, as Mordecai had written to them." (Esther 9:23). They had already started the custom, and they agreed to continue it. Agreeing is the opposite of refusing.

A lot is right, baker. The text says Haman son of Hammedatha, the Agagite, "…had cast the Pur (that is, the lot)…" Casting a lot is like pulling a name out of a hat. Haman used it as part of his plot to crush and destroy the Jews.
A net would fit a trap, so I see the thinking. But the text spells it out. Haman "…had cast the Pur (that is, the lot)…" (Esther 9:24). The parentheses give the answer, and it's a lot, not a net.

Spears do sound like what a villain would throw. But the verse says Haman "…had cast the Pur (that is, the lot)…" A lot is more like drawing a name out of a hat than hurling a weapon. The text gives the answer right there in the parentheses.

explanations.answer: It would come back on Haman's own head
explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. The king "…commanded by letter that the wicked scheme which Haman had devised against the Jews should come back upon his own head…" (Esther 9:25). The scheme Haman devised against the Jews was to come back upon his own head. That's what the king's letter commanded.

explanations.answer: It would be quietly forgotten by the court
explanations.explanation: Quietly forgotten is a fair guess, but that's not what the king commanded. He "…commanded by letter that the wicked scheme which Haman had devised against the Jews should come back upon his own head…" (Esther 9:25). The command came by letter, and it says the scheme should come back upon Haman's own head.

explanations.answer: It would go ahead exactly as planned
explanations.explanation: That would have been a very different ending, friend. But the king "…commanded by letter that the wicked scheme which Haman had devised against the Jews should come back upon his own head…" (Esther 9:25). The command is about the scheme coming back upon Haman's own head. Going ahead as planned isn't what the king's letter says.

Close, but no. The text says, "Therefore these days are called Purim, from the word Pur." (Esther 9:26). The name comes from the Pur, which is the lot Haman cast. The gallows get their own mention in the verse before it.

False is right, friend. The verse says, "Therefore these days are called Purim, from the word Pur." (Esther 9:26). The name comes from the Pur, which verse 24 says is the lot. It doesn't come from the gallows.

Descendants is right. The Jews "…bound themselves to establish the custom that they and their descendants and all who join them should not fail to celebrate these two days…" So the children and grandchildren and all the ones after them are covered. That's a family tradition built to last.

Servants is a decent guess, but that's not the word in the verse. It says "…they and their descendants and all who join them…" Descendants means the family line that comes after them. The promise was meant to be passed down.

I like the neighborly spirit, baker, but the verse uses a different word. It says "…they and their descendants and all who join them…" Descendants are the family coming down the line. Those "…who join them…" are a separate group, so there's room for company too.

The text says just the opposite. "These days should be remembered and celebrated by every generation, family, province, and city…" The aim was that "…the memory of them…" should not "…fade from their descendants." (Esther 9:28). The plan was to remember it long after the danger was over.

False is right. The text says these days "…should be remembered and celebrated by every generation, family, province, and city…" (Esther 9:28). It also says the memory should not "…fade from their descendants." This was a plan for remembering, and it was meant to go on and on.

Not quite, baker. The letters were sent "…in order to confirm these days of Purim at their appointed time…" (Esther 9:31). The days were set in advance, and the same two days applied everywhere. No city got to pick its own date.

False is right. Mordecai sent the letters "…in order to confirm these days of Purim at their appointed time…" (Esther 9:31). The date was set, so no city picked its own. Everyone was on the same calendar, from the nearest town to the farthest.

That's right, friend. "So Esther’s decree confirmed these regulations about Purim, which were written into the record." (Esther 9:32). Queen Esther's word made it official, and then it went into writing. Once something's in the record, it doesn't get lost like a recipe card in a drawer.

explanations.answer: They're read once and set aside
explanations.explanation: Once and done would be a short life for a holiday. But the verse says the regulations "…were written into the record." (Esther 9:32). A record is made to keep. Nothing here says they were set aside.

explanations.answer: They're kept secret in the palace
explanations.explanation: Secret doesn't fit what this passage describes. Mordecai sent letters to all the Jews in the 127 provinces of the kingdom (Esther 9:30). The regulations "…were written into the record." (Esther 9:32). Esther's decree confirmed them.

explanations.answer: The Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Media and Persia
explanations.explanation: Right, baker. The writer asks, "…are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Media and Persia?" (Esther 10:2). That's the book the text names for Mordecai's accomplishments and the greatness to which the king had raised him. His story is written there.

explanations.answer: The Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel
explanations.explanation: Israel's kings is a fair guess, but the verse names a different book. It says "…the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Media and Persia?" (Esther 10:2). That's where the text says Mordecai's accomplishments are written.

explanations.answer: The Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah
explanations.explanation: Judah is a fair guess, but the verse names a different book. It says "…the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Media and Persia?" (Esther 10:2). That's where the text says Mordecai's accomplishments are written.
That's right, friend. "…Mordecai the Jew was second only to King Xerxes…" (Esther 10:3). Only the king ranked above him. That's the rank the text gives him.
Governor of a single province is a fair guess, but the text gives him a different rank. Mordecai "…was second only to King Xerxes…" (Esther 10:3). Second only means just the king stood above him.

Army commander sounds impressive, and I get why you'd pick it. But the text says Mordecai "…was second only to King Xerxes…" (Esther 10:3). It doesn't say he led the army. It names his rank as second only to the king.

True, baker. Mordecai was "…seeking the good of his people and speaking peace to all his countrymen." (Esther 10:3). The same verse says he was second only to King Xerxes. Both things are said of him, and that's a good look on a powerful man.

This one is true, friend. The text says Mordecai was "…seeking the good of his people and speaking peace to all his countrymen." (Esther 10:3). The verse says that right alongside his high rank. So the statement holds.
